item.title: Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign
item.description:
Threat actors compromised 24 Check Point servers across 22 organizations in cyberespionage campaign

Threat actors exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations, according to threat intelligence firm GreyNoise. The activity, tracked as GT13, was confirmed as ongoing between October 17 and November 2, though researchers believe the campaign remains active given the threat actors’ persistent access to Check Point devices. The 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries and include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors.

🔍 Overview

The attackers launched their operations from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. GreyNoise detected the activity and noted it resembled cyberespionage operations, although the attacker’s motivation could not be conclusively determined. The researchers assessed that GT13 operated an AI-powered offensive tool, based on observed behavior, automation, and custom tooling, but this use of AI in the campaign remains unconfirmed.

🧩 How it works

The attack chain began with unknown means of initial compromise, though GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached. During post-compromise stages, the researchers observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232, an authentication bypass in Check Point SmartConsole that allows attackers to obtain an application login token and authenticate with administrator privileges. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments.

⚙️ Key details

The attackers leveraged automation and custom tooling, observed across more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 file-related activities. Their activities included:

  • Stealing firewall databases, credentials, configuration data, and internal certificate authority files
  • Generating a new certificate in one victim’s environment
  • Unloading security policies, effectively disabling firewall protections
  • Conducting internal network reconnaissance and attempting lateral movement

On October 26, the attacker performed a bulk certificate management operation across all 24 compromised Check Point servers, which failed, but still helped GreyNoise identify victims. The researchers also observed attempts to exploit multiple additional vulnerabilities: CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF), and CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script).

The campaign targeted additional enterprise systems including:

System Vulnerability Notes
Citrix NetScaler CVE-2023-4966 Targeted in lateral movement
Ivanti Connect Secure CVE-2024-21893 Targeted during campaign
VMware vCenter CVE-2021-21972, CVE-2023-34048 Multiple vulnerabilities exploited
Microsoft Exchange CVE-2021-26855/34473 Targeted during intrusions
Microsoft Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 Part of lateral movement attempts

BleepingComputer has contacted Check Point to ask if they have better visibility into those attacks and which flaw was exploited for initial access, and we are waiting for their response.

💡 Why it matters

Although GreyNoise lost visibility into the campaign operations on November 2, the researchers believe it could still be ongoing. The company has notified international government partners and CERTs to alert impacted organizations and shared indicators of compromise (IoCs) that could help identify additional intrusions or block future attempts. Check Point warned about CVE-2026-16232 in July, marking it as an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability.

The campaign demonstrates sophisticated attack capabilities using compromised infrastructure and automation tools to conduct large-scale credential theft and lateral movement across critical infrastructure sectors including government, finance, and energy.

#cybersecurity #CheckPoint #GreyNoise #GT13 #cyberespionage #AI

Source: Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations

item.title: Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler
item.description:
Critical phpAfterShell Vulnerability Disclosed in PHP Session Handler

On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a critical vulnerability in PHP’s default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. PHP released official patches to resolve this and 16 other security vulnerabilities on the same day. There is currently no indication that these vulnerabilities have been exploited in the wild.

🔍 Overview

Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, phpAfterShell scores a 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project addressed the flaw in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases also resolve 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of which are similarly rated as critical.

As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities are listed in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no reviewed sources report active exploitation.

🧩 How it works

PHP stores session data in files by default. The phpAfterShell vulnerability involves the session write and deserialization processes:

  • Session read: When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array.
  • Session write: When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.
  • Interruption: phpAfterShell is triggered when this write operation is interrupted. Following an interruption, the session file can hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the leftover end of the old session data.
  • Deserialization: On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker managed to shape the old session data, PHP can deserialize objects of the attacker’s choosing.

An attacker can shape the stored session data by using PHP’s session upload progress feature (which writes file upload progress into the session) or by targeting applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session. Although PHP notes that code execution requires a write interruption at a useful point and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application, depthfirst reports reaching code execution without any application gadget. They achieved this by chaining phpAfterShell with a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. It is unestablished whether this second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.

⚙️ Mitigation and Protection

To mitigate the vulnerability, Cloudflare has updated its Web Application Firewall (WAF) to block known phpAfterShell attack patterns. These updates build on a PHP remote code execution rule first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities, which has now been updated to cover phpAfterShell.

Rule Name / Feature Target Vulnerability Managed Ruleset Default Action
phpAfterShell Rule CVE-2026-126714 Free and Paid (Enabled by default) Block
PHP-FPM Request Smuggling Rule CVE-2026-129289 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log
PHP SOAP Extension Rules CVE-2026-15353, CVE-2026-129506 Paid Plans (Enabled by default) Log

The request smuggling and SOAP rules use the “Log” action by default because the traffic patterns they target can occasionally occur in legitimate traffic. Paid plan customers can review matching requests in Security Events and change the action to “Block” once they verify that legitimate traffic is unaffected.

Cloudflare emphasizes that the WAF serves as an additional layer of defense rather than a complete replacement for patching. Because several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or bypass pathways visible to the WAF, the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart all worker processes.

#PHP #phpAfterShell #Cybersecurity #Cloudflare #Vulnerability

Source: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws

item.title: Why Password Spreadsheets Fail to Capture Employee Credential Behavior
item.description:
Why Password Spreadsheets Fail to Capture Employee Credential Behavior

Password spreadsheets used by administrators often present a false sense of completeness, as they only reflect credentials that employees have explicitly reported, missing passwords that have been changed, created, or shared since the last update.

🔍 The Visibility Gap

Administrators may believe they have a handle on company credentials, but this view is incomplete unless someone actively updates the document. Work passwords frequently end up in untracked locations, including:

  • Browser built-in storage
  • Shared Google documents or chat messages (e.g., Slack)
  • Personal vaults used because official access is too slow
  • Sticky notes on desks

⚙️ Drivers of Unreported Use

The predominant factor in this behavior is convenience. When approved processes are slow or unclear, employees prioritize getting work done by using tools immediately at hand, even if they know it violates rules. Because employees rarely manually report every new password, update, or shared credential, these spreadsheets fail to capture the actual state of credential usage.

📊 Credential Weakness and Reuse

Lack of visibility prevents companies from knowing if critical assets are protected by weak passwords. Evidence highlights significant risks:

  • Reuse: Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found that in the median case, only 49% of users’ passwords were unique, meaning more than half were reused across services.
  • Weakness: The ‘TOP 20 Not-So-Secret Business Passwords’ report by NordPass identified ‘123456’ as the most common corporate password.
  • Complexity: Verizon’s report found that only 3% of compromised passwords in its dataset met basic complexity standards.

Without visibility into storage locations, admins cannot determine who uses a password, who it has been shared with, or if it has been changed. Consequently, they cannot assess the strength or reuse of daily credentials.

⚠️ Security Implications

If attackers gain access to a password spreadsheet, they may encrypt it for ransom or use the credentials inside to access other systems, spreading the attack further. The 2026 edition of the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report identified credential abuse as the initial access vector in 13% of breaches, while vulnerability exploitation accounted for 31%, underscoring the need for integrated credential protection.

To keep accounts protected, admins need to answer specific questions about each password: Is it strong? Who owns it? Where is it stored? Who has access? Is it reused, old, or exposed in a breach? Strong passwords are still at risk if reused across accounts, as exposure in one breach can lead to access to others.

💡 Mitigation Features

Tools like NordPass allow administrators to set password requirements to ensure strength and enable users to share credentials over protected channels. Key features include:

  • Sharing Hub: Displays who has access to passwords shared with multiple people or teams.
  • Activity Log: Records actions related to company passwords.

#PasswordManagement #Cybersecurity #CredentialSecurity #DataBreach

Source: Still tracking company passwords in spreadsheets? You’re flying blind.

item.title: Security Update Resolves Unauthorized Access in Database Registration Routing
item.description:
Security Update Resolves Unauthorized Access in Database Registration Routing

A minor security fix has been backported from version 1.0a43 to address a vulnerability that allowed unauthorized database downloads. This update resolves a security issue occurring when database routes and names do not match.

⚙️ Key details

  • Affected Registration: The issue involves databases registered using add_database(db, name=..., route=...).
  • Vulnerability Condition: The security flaw occurred when a database was registered with a route that differed from its name.
  • Access Restriction Bypass: In these instances, actors who were denied access to the database could still download it from the /<route>.db endpoint.

🚀 Availability

  • The security fix was backported from version 1.0a43.

#Cybersecurity #Database #SoftwarePatch

Source: Release: datasette 0.65.6

item.title: New Evaluation Framework for Unsupervised Narrative Label Generation
item.description:
New Evaluation Framework for Unsupervised Narrative Label Generation

Researchers have introduced a three-tier evaluation framework designed for unsupervised narrative label generation and tested it across seven disinformation datasets.

🧩 How it works

The evaluation framework consists of three tiers:

Tier Purpose
Recovery Evaluation against a corpus’s own taxonomy
Mining Evaluation against external label sets
Discovery Evaluation without predefined labels

⚙️ Key details

The study compared clustering-based and graph-community-based pipelines, finding the following:

  • Balance: In a corpus with two prominent topics, clustering can reduce one topic to 2% of generated labels, whereas graph-based pipelines remain balanced.
  • Singletons: Graph outputs produced singletons (narrative labels derived from single claims) in 30-62% of cases; clustering cannot produce these.
  • Validation: Human validation of discovery labels confirmed many singletons as recognizable disinformation narratives.

🚀 Availability

Human-validated narrative candidate labels have been released for the following datasets to support dataset extension and taxonomy development:

  • Climate Obstruction
  • PolyNarrative

#Disinformation #NarrativeLabeling #UnsupervisedLearning #DataEvaluation

Source: From Repetition to Recognition: Inductive Discovery of Disinformation Narratives
